questions.stem: Newton's FIRST Law of Motion is also known by which of the following names?
questions.explanation: Newton's First Law states: 'Every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force.' This is the LAW OF INERTIA — inertia being the property by which a body resists change in its state of rest or motion. Option A refers loosely to the Second Law (F = dp/dt). Option C is the Third Law (every action has an equal and opposite reaction). Option D is a separate Newton contribution — nothing to do with the three laws of motion.

questions.stem: A force of 20 N is applied to a body of mass 4 kg on a frictionless surface. What is the acceleration produced?
questions.explanation: By Newton's Second Law, F = ma, so a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s². Worked step by step: given F = 20 N, m = 4 kg. Rearranging F = ma → a = F/m = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s². Distractor 2 m/s² would be (force − mass)/something — pure error; 80 m/s² comes from 20×4 (multiplying instead of dividing — a common slip); 24 m/s² comes from 20+4 (adding instead of dividing — less common but tracks a student who has forgotten the formula entirely).

questions.stem: When a rifle is fired, the rifle RECOILS backward. This illustrates which of Newton's laws?
questions.explanation: The forward force exerted on the bullet by the rifle PRODUCES an equal and opposite backward force on the rifle — pure Newton's Third Law ('every action has an equal and opposite reaction'). Rocket propulsion uses the same principle. Other common Third Law illustrations: walking (feet push ground back, ground pushes us forward), swimming (arms push water back, water pushes swimmer forward), a bird flying (wings push air down, air pushes bird up). The First Law explains why a stationary rifle stays stationary until fired. The Second Law quantifies the recoil velocity using momentum conservation.

questions.stem: A bus moving at 20 m/s suddenly brakes and comes to rest in 4 seconds. If its mass is 2000 kg, what is the magnitude of the AVERAGE braking force?
questions.explanation: Step-by-step: (1) Acceleration a = (v − u)/t = (0 − 20)/4 = −5 m/s² — magnitude 5 m/s². (2) By Newton's Second Law, F = ma = 2000 × 5 = 10 000 N (taking magnitudes). The direction is opposite to the motion (braking). Distractor 5 000 N drops the mass by a factor of 2 (common slip: thinking mass = 1000 kg). 40 000 N mistakenly multiplies by 4 (the time) instead of dividing. 2 500 N divides the mass by the time (nonsensical dimensionally). Always unit-check: N = kg·m/s² — so 2000 × 5 = 10 000 N checks out.

questions.stem: The momentum of a body is defined as:
questions.explanation: Momentum p = m·v. Since velocity is a vector, momentum is a vector. Unit: kg·m/s (or N·s). Newton's Second Law in its ORIGINAL form: F = dp/dt (rate of change of momentum = force). When mass is constant, this simplifies to F = ma. Option B is force F = ma (not momentum). Option C has wrong units and definition. Option D confuses with kinetic energy which is (1/2)mv² (a scalar).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Two bodies of masses 4 kg and 6 kg moving in the same direction with velocities 10 m/s and 5 m/s respectively collide. If they STICK TOGETHER after collision, their common velocity is (assume perfectly inelastic collision, no external forces):
questions.explanation: By conservation of momentum: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)V. Plugging in: 4(10) + 6(5) = (4+6)V → 40 + 30 = 10V → 70 = 10V → V = 7 m/s. (Derivation shown step-by-step; answer matches option B exactly.) Distractor 5 m/s is simply the slower body's speed (ignoring the collision); 15 m/s is the sum of speeds (nonsense); 10 m/s is the faster body's speed. Momentum conservation — not energy conservation — is what always holds in collisions without external force. Energy is NOT conserved in inelastic collisions (some becomes heat/deformation).

questions.stem: Which statement about the three types of friction — STATIC, KINETIC, and ROLLING — is CORRECT?

options.option_text: Kinetic friction > Static friction > Rolling friction
Static friction (maximum) > Kinetic friction > Rolling friction
All three are always equal in magnitude
Rolling friction > Kinetic friction > Static friction

questions.explanation: The CORRECT ordering (for the same surfaces and normal force): μ_s (static, maximum) > μ_k (kinetic) > μ_r (rolling). This is why: (i) it takes more force to START pushing a box than to keep it sliding (static > kinetic); (ii) wheels and ball-bearings are used because rolling friction is FAR smaller than sliding/kinetic friction. For typical steel-on-steel: μ_s ≈ 0.74, μ_k ≈ 0.57, μ_r (rolling) ≈ 0.002. This vast gap between kinetic and rolling friction is why the wheel is one of humanity's most impactful inventions.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A block of mass 5 kg is kept on a horizontal surface with coefficient of static friction μ_s = 0.4. What is the MINIMUM horizontal force needed to JUST START moving the block? (Take g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: The block JUST starts moving when applied force equals the maximum static friction. Step 1: Normal force N = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N (the block rests on a horizontal surface, so N balances weight). Step 2: Maximum static friction f_s_max = μ_s · N = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N. Step 3: Applied force needed = 20 N (just enough to overcome static friction). Distractor 10 N is half — maybe from μ_s · mg/2 confusion. 50 N is just N (student forgot to multiply by μ). 2 N is μ_s · m without g — dimensional error.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a practical application of Newton's FIRST Law of Motion?

options.option_text: Firing a bullet from a gun producing recoil
Seat belts in cars preventing passengers from continuing forward when the car suddenly stops
Using a hydraulic lift to raise heavy objects
Calculating the acceleration of a falling body

questions.explanation: When a car suddenly brakes, the PASSENGERS' upper bodies continue moving forward at the original velocity (by inertia / First Law) — the seat belt applies the external force that brings them to rest, preventing collision with the windshield. Classic First-Law application. Option A demonstrates the Third Law (action-reaction). Option C is based on Pascal's principle (fluid pressure transmission), not Newton's laws directly. Option D uses the Second Law (F = ma, with F = mg). Other everyday First-Law examples: dust flying off a shaken carpet, a fruit falling from a tree when its branch is shaken, a standing passenger in a bus jerking backward when the bus accelerates forward.

questions.stem: In the expression F = ma, all units are SI. Which of the following is the CORRECT SI unit breakdown of the newton (N)?
questions.explanation: 1 newton = 1 kg · m / s² (unit of mass × unit of acceleration). This is the standard SI unit check for any physics problem involving force. Option A omits the meter (wrong dimension). Option C has the wrong time-exponent (time should be in the denominator with exponent 2). Option D is the unit of ENERGY — the joule (1 J = 1 kg·m²/s²) — not force. Always unit-check answers: if your final numeric result has dimensions that don't match what the question asks, the computation is wrong.

questions.stem: Two astronauts in space — far from any gravitational body and initially at rest — push off from each other. If astronaut A (60 kg) moves off at 2 m/s, what is the velocity of astronaut B (80 kg)?

options.option_text: 2.0 m/s in the same direction as A
1.5 m/s in the opposite direction to A
2.67 m/s in the opposite direction to A
0 m/s — A's velocity alone satisfies momentum conservation

questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum: initial total momentum = 0 (both at rest). After pushing off, momenta must still sum to zero → m_A · v_A + m_B · v_B = 0. So v_B = −(m_A / m_B) · v_A = −(60/80) × 2 = −1.5 m/s. The negative sign means OPPOSITE direction — so B moves at 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction. Distractor C (2.67) swaps the mass ratio: v_B = −(80/60) × 2 = −2.67 — a very common error. A is nonsensical (violates momentum conservation). D forgets that conservation applies to the system, not to a single body alone.

questions.stem: The coefficient of friction between two surfaces is a DIMENSIONLESS number because:

options.option_text: It is defined as the ratio of two forces (friction / normal), so the units cancel
It is a probability value between 0 and 1
It is computed using only integer counting
It is always exactly equal to 1 in SI

questions.explanation: μ = f / N where f is the friction force and N the normal force — both in newtons. Ratio of two quantities with identical units is DIMENSIONLESS. Typical values: rubber on dry concrete ≈ 1.0; steel on steel ≈ 0.57 (kinetic); ice on ice ≈ 0.03; rolling friction for ball-bearings ≈ 0.001. Although μ is typically between 0 and 1, μ > 1 IS possible (e.g. some rubber-on-rubber can reach ~1.2-1.5). Option B is a conceptual misconception — μ is NOT a probability. Option C is wrong — it's a real-valued ratio. Option D is wrong — it varies widely.

questions.stem: When a body slides down an INCLINED plane at a constant velocity, the relationship between the angle of inclination θ and the coefficient of kinetic friction μ_k is:
questions.explanation: At CONSTANT velocity down an incline, net force = 0. Forces along the incline: component of gravity down the slope = mg sin θ; friction up the slope = μ_k · N = μ_k · mg cos θ. Setting them equal: mg sin θ = μ_k · mg cos θ → μ_k = sin θ / cos θ = TAN θ. The angle at which this happens is called the 'angle of friction' or 'angle of repose'. Typical engineering: a steel coil on a wooden ramp slides at ~30° → μ ≈ tan 30° ≈ 0.58. The distractors sin θ and cos θ reflect common slips (student forgets to take both components).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the CORRECT description of Galileo's contribution to the study of motion, later formalised by Newton?

options.option_text: Galileo proved that heavier bodies fall faster than lighter ones
Galileo showed that in the ABSENCE of air resistance, all bodies fall with the same acceleration
Galileo invented the calculus used to derive F = ma
Galileo discovered the universal law of gravitation

questions.explanation: Galileo's famous (possibly apocryphal) Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment and his inclined-plane experiments showed that heavier and lighter bodies fall with the SAME acceleration when air resistance is negligible — refuting the Aristotelian view that heavier bodies fall faster (option A, which Galileo DISPROVED). This was foundational for Newton's First and Second Laws. Newton and Leibniz independently invented calculus (not Galileo). Newton's universal law of gravitation came later in Principia (1687). A classic 1971 demonstration: Apollo 15 astronaut Dave Scott dropped a hammer and feather on the airless Moon — they hit the surface simultaneously.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios INCREASES friction, useful in many practical applications?

options.option_text: Lubrication of machine parts with oil
Polishing a surface to be smooth
Using treaded tyres on vehicles and grooves on shoe soles
Using ball-bearings in the wheels of a car

questions.explanation: Treaded tyres and soled shoes INCREASE friction — critical for vehicle braking/cornering and for walking without slipping on wet surfaces. Options A (lubrication), B (polishing), and D (ball-bearings — which convert sliding to rolling friction) all DECREASE friction. A balanced understanding of friction recognises both: we WANT friction for driving/walking, BUT also want to REDUCE it in moving engine parts and bearings. Treads work by channeling water away from the contact patch, preventing hydroplaning. Racing slicks (no treads) have MORE rubber-on-road contact in dry conditions — a specialized case — but are illegal in rain.
